source.title: Revisiting Distributed Synchronous SGD
source.authors: Jian-Min Chen; Xing-Hao Pan; Rajat Monga; Samy Bengio; R. Józefowicz

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies synchronous worker counts, which scale effective batch size, reports test-performance results, and says it did not observe the large-batch generalization effect. Its comparisons do not hold the epoch budget fixed as V5 specifies.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results about staleness, convergence speed, and stragglers; these do not measure the claim versions. Figure-only values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study discusses the large-batch generalization penalty, but its results compare synchronous and asynchronous training at convergence, without a fixed data-epoch budget. Synchronization changes gradient staleness, and Inception also uses learning-rate scaling and different clipping. These comparisons do not establish whether V5 holds.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: synchronous optimization with backup workers improves reported test performance over asynchronous training. The authors report no observed large-batch generalization penalty and suggest their experiments remain below the relevant batch-size regime; this does not establish a challenge to V5.
record.recipe_differences: Uses distributed Sync-Opt and Async-Opt comparisons with RMSProp on Inception and PixelCNN; varies worker counts and does not isolate the fixed-epoch batch-size comparison in V5.
record.method_sensitivity: Worker count and synchronization mode vary; the paper says the large-batch effect was not observed in its experimental regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Synchronous training achieves approximately 0.5 percentage-point better ImageNet test precision than asynchronous training at comparable worker counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distributed synchronization choices can affect held-out performance through gradient staleness and associated training-recipe differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Synchronous PixelCNN training achieves lower test NLL than asynchronous training; asynchronous performance deteriorates as worker count increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Asynchronous distributed training can degrade image-generation performance as gradient staleness increases.

record.peer_reviewed: under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2017
record.problems: The relevant comparisons do not hold the epoch budget fixed as V5 specifies. The test-performance values are not given numerically in the prose, and the batch-size regime is not characterized beyond the authors' statement that they did not reach the regime examined by Keskar et al.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-version results were found. Other reported results concern staleness, convergence time, and straggler effects, which do not measure the versions.

untested.parts: Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed data-epoch budgets and controlled comparisons of recipe adaptations. Inception already uses learning-rate scaling, but its contribution is not isolated.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'epoch' in Section 4.2 means a synchronous iteration or N asynchronous updates, rather than a complete dataset pass. Its convergence comparisons therefore should not be read as fixed data-epoch comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep past the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD.
Fixed-epoch-budget comparisons; language models; recipe adaptations such as longer training, learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: Inception
rows.operation_detail: Compared Sync-Opt and Async-Opt test precision across worker configurations.
rows.value: Sync-Opt attained ∼0.5% better test precision for comparable N+b workers.
rows.note: The text reports the comparison in aggregate; it does not state per-configuration values. The comparison is not described as holding the epoch budget fixed.
rows.check: The approximately 0.5 percentage-point precision advantage is correctly reported, but compares the study's synchronous method with asynchronous training. Staleness, learning rates and clipping differ; training budgets are not fixed. It cannot establish a reversed batch-size penalty.

rows.subject: PixelCNN
rows.operation_detail: Compared Sync-Opt and Async-Opt test negative log likelihood across worker configurations.
rows.measure: Test negative log likelihood (lower is better)
rows.value: Sync-Opt obtains lower NLL than Async-Opt.
rows.note: The paper does not provide numerical NLL values in the prose for this comparison or state that epochs are held fixed.
rows.check: Lower test NLL for synchronous training is correctly reported, but measures synchronization-method performance in an image-generation model, rather than a fixed-budget batch-size effect in image classification or language modeling. It cannot establish a reversed V5 effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Inception and PixelCNN comparisons in the reported configurations
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that they did not observe the large-batch generalization effect; Sync-Opt also had better reported test performance than Async-Opt in these comparisons (R1, R2). These results do not use a fixed-epoch-budget comparison.
